# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and Definition

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterised by delayed opacification of the distal coronary vasculature in the absence of significant epicardial coronary stenosis. Coronary slow flow phenomenon, also known as cardiac syndrome Y, is characterised by angiographically normal or near-normal coronary arteries with delayed opacification of the distal vasculature. The entity was first described more than five decades ago, when Tambe, Demany, Zimmerman, and Mascarenhas reported angina pectoris and slow flow velocity of dye in coronary arteries as a new angiographic finding in the American Heart Journal in 1972. Far from being a benign curiosity, CSFP carries genuine clinical consequences, with patients presenting with chest pain, acute coronary syndromes, arrhythmias, and even sudden death [3].

The disorder is now regarded as a primary microvascular condition. CSF is currently characterized as a primary microvascular disease that is indicated by heightened resistance to coronary flow and slowed filling of the coronaries without associated obstructive artery disease. A seminal characterisation came from Beltrame and colleagues, who proposed that the coronary slow flow phenomenon is an angiographic finding characterized by delayed distal vessel opacification in the absence of significant epicardial coronary disease. In their case-control study, patients with coronary slow flow differed from controls, more often being current smokers and presenting with rest pain requiring urgent admission, usually to the coronary care unit.

## Epidemiology

CSFP is encountered relatively frequently during diagnostic angiography. The prevalence ranges from 1–5% of coronary angiograms and it is more frequent in young male smokers. In a large series, CSFP was identified in 96 (5.5%) subjects referred for coronary angiography, and was associated with male sex and obesity. Hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and tobacco use feature prominently among associated risk factors; in one cohort, acute coronary syndrome was the most common mode of presentation, and hypertension, dyslipidaemia, smoking and tobacco chewing were considered independent risk factors for the phenomenon.

## Diagnosis

Diagnosis rests on angiographic quantification of coronary flow. The semi-quantitative TIMI flow grade was an early tool, but objective standardisation came with the corrected TIMI frame count (cTFC) introduced by Gibson et al. Although the TIMI flow grade is a valuable and widely used qualitative measure in angiographic trials, it is limited by its subjective and categorical nature; the number of cineframes needed for dye to reach standardised distal landmarks objectively assesses coronary blood flow as a continuous variable. Because the left anterior descending artery is longer, the longer LAD frame counts were corrected by dividing by 1.7 to derive the corrected TIMI frame count (CTFC). In practice, diagnosis of CSFP is made angiographically with demonstration of either TIMI-2 flow or a corrected TIMI frame count of >27 frames, in addition to no angiographic lesions ≥40% and delayed distal vessel opacification in at least one epicardial vessel. The COVADIS consensus has incorporated this concept; the 2018 consensus statement requires symptoms and objective signs of myocardial ischaemia, an absence of coronary obstruction, and at least one of low coronary flow reserve, elevated microcirculatory resistance, microvascular spasm, or the coronary slow-flow phenomenon defined by a corrected TIMI frame count >25. However, recent invasive physiological work cautions that coronary slow flow phenomenon defined by corrected TFC >27 was a poor indicator of coronary microvascular dysfunction in some populations, whereas other data show that CSFP was associated with low flow velocity and higher microvascular resistance at rest compared with patients without CSFP. Non-invasively, transthoracic Doppler echocardiography is emerging, since patients with CSFP exhibit lower coronary diastolic velocities of the LAD, which are negatively correlated with cTFC.

## Pathophysiology

The mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Although it is well known to interventional cardiologists for approximately four decades, the pathogenic mechanisms remain unclear, while clinical implications are significant, with over 80% of patients experiencing recurrent chest pain. Several overlapping processes have been implicated. Histopathological studies showed small-vessel abnormalities; CSFP patients display small vessel thickening with luminal narrowing, dilated interstitial spaces, decreased intracellular glycogen, distorted mitochondrial cristae and patchy myofibrillar disarray, suggesting that fibromuscular hyperplasia and medial hypertrophy with consequent decrease in luminal diameter lead to functional obstruction.

Endothelial dysfunction is a central theme. In one study, endothelin-1 and nitric oxide concentrations were assessed in slow coronary flow patients before and at peak exercise and compared with healthy controls, with a mean TIMI frame count of 54.1 in patients. Inflammation also contributes; increased high-sensitivity CRP levels have been reported and implicated in the pathogenesis of slow coronary flow. A more recent meta-analysis confirmed that a significant association exists between CSF and hs-CRP. Other markers, including the systemic immune-inflammation index, support an inflammatory basis; patients with CSF had higher SII, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, and hsCRP levels compared with controls. Elevated homocysteine has likewise been described in this population [27]. Diffuse subclinical atherosclerosis may coexist, and impaired glucose metabolism has been linked to CSFP [28].

## Clinical Course and Prognosis

While historically considered benign, CSFP causes substantial morbidity. CSF is clinically relevant, with patients presenting with chest pain, arrhythmias, and even sudden death, and therefore markedly impairs quality of life. In a large prospective cohort, 429 patients fulfilling CSFP criteria were followed for a mean of 3.8 years, with major adverse cardiovascular events occurring in 39 patients (9.3%).

## Management

No uniformly effective therapy exists. CSFP does not have an effective and uniform treatment; it produces chest pain and reduces quality of life, although medicines such as nebivolol, atorvastatin, mibefradil, nitroglycerin and nicorandil have been reported to be effective in reducing symptoms. The calcium T-channel blocker mibefradil showed benefit; compared with placebo, mibefradil significantly reduced total angina frequency by 56%, prolonged episodes of angina by 74%, and sublingual nitrate consumption by 59%, and improved physical quality of life. Nebivolol improves endothelial function: nebivolol is effective at improving endothelial function in patients with SCF, controls chest pain, decreases CRP, and has favourable effects on brachial artery dilation variables. Vasodilators acting on the microcirculation are also useful, since dipyridamole abolishes functional obstruction in coronary arteries with diameters less than 200 micrometres and is considered superior in treating CSFP compared with nitroglycerine. Statins may confer pleiotropic benefit, and Cakmak et al. concluded that 40 mg simvastatin improved myocardial perfusion in patients with CSF. Novel endothelin-receptor antagonism is under investigation; a randomised trial evaluated the impact of a 10 mg daily dose of zibotentan on spontaneous angina episodes in patients with coronary slow-flow phenomenon who had refractory angina.

## Conclusion

CSFP is a clinically relevant microvascular disorder that should not be dismissed as an incidental angiographic observation. CSFP should be considered as a pathological entity and not an entirely benign condition. Its pathophysiology spans endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, small-vessel structural change, and microvascular dysregulation. Standardised invasive and non-invasive diagnostic criteria, alongside well-powered randomised therapeutic trials, are needed to improve recognition and management of affected patients [3].
